{{Short description|none}}
{{hatnote|This article is about mathematical proofs that are incomplete or incorrect in some way. They are not to be confused with mathematical proofs pertaining to the ''topic'' of incompleteness, such as [[Gödel's incompleteness theorems]] etc.}}

{{quote box
|align =right
|width =40%
|quote = A technical argument by a trusted author, which is hard to check and looks similar to arguments known to be correct, is hardly ever checked in detail.
|author = [[Vladimir Voevodsky]]
|source =<ref name="vladimir" />
}}

This page lists notable examples of incomplete or incorrect published [[mathematical proof]]s. Most of these were accepted as complete or correct for several years but later discovered to contain gaps or errors. There are both examples where a complete proof was later found, or where the alleged result turned out to be false.

==Results later proved rigorously==
* [[Euclid's Elements|Euclid's ''Elements'']]. Euclid's proofs are essentially correct, but strictly speaking sometimes contain gaps because he tacitly uses some unstated assumptions, such as the existence of [[Line–line intersection|intersection points]]. In 1899 [[David Hilbert]] gave a complete set of ([[second-order logic|second order]]) axioms for Euclidean geometry, called [[Hilbert's axioms]], and between 1926 and 1959 [[Alfred Tarski|Tarski]] gave some complete sets of [[First-order logic|first order axioms]], called [[Tarski's axioms]].
* [[Isoperimetric inequality]]. For three dimensions it states that the shape enclosing the maximum volume for its surface area is the sphere. It was formulated by [[Archimedes]] but not proved rigorously until the 19th century, by [[Hermann Schwarz]].
* [[Infinitesimals]]. In the 18th century there was widespread use of infinitesimals in calculus, though these were not really well defined. Calculus was put on firm foundations in the 19th century, and [[Abraham Robinson|Robinson]] put infinitesimals in a rigorous basis with the introduction of [[nonstandard analysis]] in the 20th century.
* [[Fundamental theorem of algebra]] (see [[Fundamental theorem of algebra#History|History]]).  Many incomplete or incorrect attempts were made at proving this theorem in the 18th century, including by [[Jean le Rond d'Alembert|d'Alembert]] (1746), [[Leonhard Euler|Euler]] (1749), [[François Daviet de Foncenex|de Foncenex]] (1759), [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange|Lagrange]] (1772), [[Pierre-Simon Laplace|Laplace]] (1795), [[James Wood (mathematician)|Wood]] (1798), and [[Johann Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]] (1799).  The first rigorous proof was published by [[Jean-Robert Argand|Argand]] in 1806.
* [[Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions]]. In 1808 Legendre published an attempt at a proof of Dirichlet's theorem, but as Dupré pointed out in 1859 one of the lemmas used by Legendre is false. [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet|Dirichlet]] gave a complete proof in 1837.
* The proofs of the [[Kronecker–Weber theorem]] by [[Leopold Kronecker|Kronecker]] (1853) and [[Heinrich Martin Weber|Weber]] (1886) both had gaps. The first complete proof was given by Hilbert in 1896.
* In 1879, [[Alfred Kempe]] published a purported proof of the [[four color theorem]], whose validity as a proof was accepted for eleven years before it was refuted by [[Percy Heawood]]. [[Peter Guthrie Tait]] gave another incorrect proof in 1880 which was shown to be incorrect by [[Julius Petersen]] in 1891. Kempe's proof did, however, suffice to show the weaker [[five color theorem]]. The four-color theorem was eventually proved by [[Kenneth Appel]] and [[Wolfgang Haken]] in 1976.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Saaty |first1=Thomas L. |author-link=Thomas L. Saaty |title=The four-color problem: assaults and conquest |last2=Kainen |first2=Paul C. |author-link2=Paul Chester Kainen |publisher=Dover Publications |year=1986 |isbn=978-0-486-65092-0 |location=New York}}</ref>
*  [[Schröder–Bernstein theorem]]. In 1896 [[Ernst Schröder (mathematician)|Schröder]] published a proof sketch<ref>{{Cite book |last=Schröder |first=Ernst |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/45265#page/331/mode/1up |title=Ueber zwei Definitionen der Endlichkeit und G. Cantor'sche Sätze |publisher=Johann Ambrosius Barth Verlag |year=1898 |editor-last=Kaiserliche Leopoldino-Carolinische Deutsche Akademie der Naturforscher |volume=71 |pages=303–376 (proof: p.336–344) |issue=6}}</ref> which, however, was shown to be faulty by [[Alwin Reinhold Korselt]] in 1911<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Korselt |first=A. |date=June 1911 |editor2-last=Walther von Dyck |editor3-last=David Hilbert |editor4-last=Otto Blumenthal |title=Über einen Beweis des Äquivalenzsatzes |url=http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/dms/load/img/?PPN=PPN235181684_0070&DMDID=DMDLOG_0029 |journal=Mathematische Annalen |language=de |location=Leipzig |publisher=B. G. Teubner |volume=70 |issue=2 |pages=294–296 |doi=10.1007/BF01461161 |issn=0025-5831 |s2cid=119757900 |editor-first=Felix |editor-last=Klein}}</ref> (confirmed by Schröder).<ref name="Brieskorn.Chatterji.2002">{{Cite book |last1=Hausdorff |first1=Felix |author-link=Felix Hausdorff |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3nth_p-6DpcC |title=Gesammelte Werke: einschliesslich der under dem Pseudonym Paul Mongré erschienenen philosophischen und literarischen Schriften und ausgewählter Texte aus dem Nachlass |last2=Brieskorn |first2=Egbert |date=2001 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-642-25598-4 |edition=1. |location=Berlin; New York |pages=587 |oclc=ocm57368353}} – [https://jscholarship.library.jhu.edu/handle/1774.2/34091 Original edition (1914)]</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Korselt|1911|p=295}}</ref>
* [[Fermat's Last Theorem]]. An initial proof was released by [[Andrew Wiles]] in June 1993 but was found to contain an error in September of that year.<ref>{{cite news|last=Kolata|first=Gina|title=At Last, Shout of 'Eureka!' In Age-Old Math Mystery|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/06/24/us/at-last-shout-of-eureka-in-age-old-math-mystery.html|access-date=21 January 2013|newspaper=The New York Times|date=24 June 1993|archive-date=26 July 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230726152255/https://www.nytimes.com/1993/06/24/us/at-last-shout-of-eureka-in-age-old-math-mystery.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Wiles would go on to publish a [[Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem|corrected proof]] in 1995.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.abelprize.no/c67107/binfil/download.php?tid=67059|title=The Abel Prize 2016|date=2016|website=Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters|access-date=29 June 2017|archive-date=20 May 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200520195920/https://www.abelprize.no/c67107/binfil/download.php?tid=67059|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* [[Jordan curve theorem]]. There has been some controversy about whether Jordan's original proof of this in 1887 contains gaps. [[Oswald Veblen]] in 1905 claimed that Jordan's proof is incomplete, but in 2007 [[Thomas Callister Hales|Hales]]  said that the gaps are minor and that Jordan's proof is essentially complete.
* In 1905 [[Henri Lebesgue|Lebesgue]] tried to prove the (correct) result that a function implicitly defined by a [[Baire function]] is Baire, but his proof incorrectly assumed that the [[projection (measure theory)|projection]] of a [[Borel set]] is Borel. [[Mikhail Yakovlevich Suslin|Suslin]] pointed out the error and was inspired by it to define [[analytic set]]s as continuous [[Image (mathematics)|images]] of Borel sets.
* [[Dehn's lemma]]. [[Max Dehn|Dehn]] published an attempted proof in 1910, but [[Hellmuth Kneser|Kneser]] found a gap in 1929. It was finally proved in 1956 by [[Christos Papakyriakopoulos]].
* [[Hilbert's sixteenth problem]] about the finiteness of the number of limit cycles of a plane polynomial vector field. [[Henri Dulac]] published a partial solution to this problem in 1923, but in about 1980 [[Jean Écalle|Écalle]] and [[Yulij Ilyashenko|Ilyashenko]] independently found a serious gap, and fixed it in about 1991.<ref name=ilu>{{cite journal|author=Yulij Ilyashenko|title=Centennial History of Hilbert's 16th problem|journal=Bulletin of the AMS|year=2002|volume=39|issue=3|pages=301–354|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/2002-39-03/S0273-0979-02-00946-1/S0273-0979-02-00946-1.pdf|doi=10.1090/s0273-0979-02-00946-1|doi-access=free}}</ref>
* In 1929 [[Lazar Lyusternik]] and [[Lev Schnirelmann]] published a proof of the [[theorem of the three geodesics]], which was later found to be flawed. The proof was completed by [[Hans Werner Ballmann|Werner Ballmann]] about 50 years later.
* [[Littlewood–Richardson rule]]. [[Gilbert de Beauregard Robinson|Robinson]] published an incomplete proof in 1938, though the gaps were not noticed for many years. The first complete proofs were given by [[Marcel-Paul Schützenberger]] in 1977  and Thomas in 1974.
* [[Class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields]]. In 1952 [[Kurt Heegner|Heegner]] published a solution to this problem. His paper was not accepted as a complete proof as it contained a gap, and the first complete proofs were given in about 1967 by [[Alan Baker (mathematician)|Baker]] and [[Harold Stark|Stark]]. In 1969 Stark showed how to fill the gap in Heegner's paper.
* In 1954 [[Igor Shafarevich]] published a proof that [[Shafarevich's theorem on solvable Galois groups|every finite solvable group is a Galois group over the rationals]]. However [[Alexander Schmidt (mathematician)|Schmidt]] pointed out a gap in the argument at the [[prime number|prime]] 2, which Shafarevich fixed in 1989.
* [[Nielsen realization problem]]. Kravetz claimed to solve this in 1959 by first showing that [[Teichmüller space]] is negatively curved, but in 1974 [[Howard Masur|Masur]] showed that it is not negatively curved. The Nielsen realization problem was finally solved in 1980 by [[Steven Kerckhoff|Kerckhoff]].
* [[Yamabe problem]]. [[Hidehiko Yamabe|Yamabe]] claimed  a solution in 1960, but [[Neil Trudinger|Trudinger]] discovered a gap in 1968, and a complete proof was not given until 1984.
* [[Mordell conjecture]] over [[Global function field|function field]]s. [[Yuri I. Manin|Manin]] published a proof in 1963, but {{harvtxt|Coleman|1990}} found and corrected a gap in the proof.
* In 1973 [[John Britton (mathematician)|Britton]] published a 282-page attempted solution of [[Burnside's problem]]. In his proof he assumed the existence of a set of parameters satisfying some inequalities, but [[Sergei Adian|Adian]] pointed out that these inequalities were inconsistent. [[Pyotr Novikov|Novikov]] and Adian had previously found a correct solution around 1968.
* [[Classification of finite simple groups]]. In 1983, [[Daniel Gorenstein|Gorenstein]] announced that the proof of the classification had been completed, but he had been misinformed about the status of the proof of classification of [[quasithin group]]s, which had a serious gap in it. A complete proof for this case was published by [[Michael Aschbacher|Aschbacher]] and Smith in 2004.
*In 1986, [[Spencer Bloch]] published the paper "Algebraic Cycles and Higher K-theory" which introduced a [[higher Chow group]], a precursor to [[motivic cohomology]]. The paper used an incorrect moving lemma; the lemma was later replaced by 30 pages of complex arguments that "took many years to be accepted as correct."<ref name="vladimir">{{Cite web |last=Voevodsky |first=Vladimir |author-link=Vladimir Voevodsky |date=March 26, 2014 |title=Univalent Foundations |url=https://www.math.ias.edu/~vladimir/Site3/Univalent_Foundations_files/2014_IAS.pdf |website=[[Institute for Advanced Study]]}}</ref>
* [[Kepler conjecture]]. Hsiang published an incomplete proof of this in 1993. In 1998 [[Thomas Callister Hales|Hales]] published a proof depending on long computer calculations.

==Incorrect results==
* In 1759 Euler claimed that there were no closed [[knight's tour|knight tour]]s on a chess board with 3 rows, but in 1917 Ernest Bergholt found  tours on 3 × 10 and 3 × 12 boards.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Zubkov | first1 = A. M. | year = 2011 | title = Euler and combinatorial calculus | journal = Proceedings of the Steklov Institute of Mathematics | volume = 274 | pages = 162–168 | doi=10.1134/s0081543811070030| s2cid = 121881906 }}</ref>
* Euler's conjecture on [[Graeco-Latin square]]s. In the 1780s Euler conjectured that no such squares exist for any oddly even number ''n'' ≡ 2 (mod 4). In 1959, [[Raj Chandra Bose|R. C. Bose]] and [[Sharadchandra Shankar Shrikhande|S. S. Shrikhande]] constructed [[counterexample]]s of order 22. Then [[E. T. Parker]] found a counterexample of order 10 using a one-hour computer search. Finally Parker, Bose, and Shrikhande showed this conjecture to be false for all ''n'' ≥ 10.
* In 1798 [[A. M. Legendre]] claimed that 6 is not the sum of 2 rational cubes,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Legendre |first=Adrien-Marie |author-link=Adrien-Marie Legendre |url=https://archive.org/details/essaisurlathor00lege |title=Essai sur la théorie des nombres |date=1798 |publisher=Duprat |location=Paris}}</ref> which as [[Gabriel Lamé|Lamé]] pointed out in 1865 is false as 6&nbsp;=&nbsp;(37/21)<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;(17/21)<sup>3</sup>.
* In 1803, [[Gian Francesco Malfatti]] claimed to prove that a certain arrangement of three circles would cover the maximum possible area inside a right triangle.  However, to do so he made certain unwarranted assumptions about the configuration of the circles.  It was shown in 1930 that circles in a different configuration could cover a greater area, and in 1967 that Malfatti's configuration was ''never'' optimal.  See [[Malfatti circles]].
* In 1806 [[André-Marie Ampère]] claimed to prove that a [[continuous function]] is [[differentiable function|differentiable]] at most points (though it is not entirely clear what he was claiming as he did not give a precise definition of a function).  However, in 1872 [[Karl Weierstrass|Weierstrass]] gave an example of a continuous function that was not differentiable anywhere: The [[Weierstrass function]].
* [[Intersection theory]]. In 1848 [[Jakob Steiner|Steiner]] claimed that [[Steiner's conic problem|the number of conics tangent to 5 given conics]] is 7776&nbsp;=&nbsp;6<sup>5</sup>, but later realized this was wrong. The correct number 3264 was found by Berner in 1865 and by [[Ernest de Jonquieres]] around 1859 and by [[Michel Chasles|Chasles]] in 1864 using his theory of characteristics. However these results, like many others in classical intersection theory, do not seem to have been given complete proofs until the work of [[William Fulton (mathematician)|Fulton]] and [[Robert MacPherson (mathematician)|Macpherson]] in about 1978.
* [[Dirichlet's principle]]. This was used by [[Bernhard Riemann|Riemann]] in 1851, but Weierstrass found a counterexample to one version of this principle in 1870, and Hilbert stated and proved a correct version in 1900.
* {{harvs|txt|last=[[Arthur Cayley|Cayley]]|year=1878}} incorrectly claimed that there are three different [[group (mathematics)|groups]] of [[order (group theory)|order]] 6. This mistake is strange because in an earlier 1854 paper he correctly stated that there are just two such groups.
* In 1885, [[Evgraf Fedorov]] classified the [[convex polyhedra]] with congruent rhombic faces, but missed a case. [[Stanko Bilinski]] in 1960 rediscovered the [[Bilinski dodecahedron]] (forgotten after its previous 1752 publication) and proved that, with the addition of this shape, the classification was complete.<ref name="grun">{{citation
 |last        = Grünbaum
 |first       = Branko
 |author-link  = Branko Grünbaum
 |doi         = 10.1007/s00283-010-9138-7
 |issue       = 4
 |journal     = [[The Mathematical Intelligencer]]
 |mr          = 2747698
 |pages       = 5–15
 |title       = The Bilinski dodecahedron and assorted parallelohedra, zonohedra, monohedra, isozonohedra, and otherhedra
 |url         = https://dlib.lib.washington.edu/researchworks/bitstream/handle/1773/15593/Bilinski_dodecahedron.pdf
 |volume      = 32
 |year        = 2010
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20150402132516/https://dlib.lib.washington.edu/researchworks/bitstream/handle/1773/15593/Bilinski_dodecahedron.pdf
 |archive-date = 2015-04-02
|hdl = 1773/15593
 |s2cid = 120403108
 |hdl-access= free
 }}.</ref>
* [[Wronskian]]s. In 1887 [[Paul Mansion|Mansion]] claimed in his textbook that if a Wronskian of some functions vanishes everywhere then the functions are linearly dependent. In 1889 Peano pointed out the counterexample ''x''<sup>2</sup> and ''x''|''x''|. The result is correct if the functions are [[analytic function|analytic]].
* {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Theodor Vahlen|last=Vahlen|year=1891}} published a purported example of an [[algebraic curve]] in 3-dimensional [[projective space]] that could not be defined as the [[zero of a function|zeros]] of 3 polynomials, but in 1941 [[Oskar Perron|Perron]] found 3 equations defining Vahlen's curve. In 1961 [[Martin Kneser|Kneser]] showed that any algebraic curve in projective 3-space can be given as the zeros of 3 polynomials.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://mathoverflow.net/q/35476 |title = Ho.history overview - Widely accepted mathematical results that were later shown to be wrong?}}</ref>
* In 1898 [[George Abram Miller|Miller]] published a paper incorrectly claiming to prove that the [[Mathieu group]] M<sub>24</sub> does not exist, though in 1900 he pointed out that his proof was wrong.
* [[Charles Newton Little|Little]] claimed in 1900 that the [[writhe]] of a reduced knot diagram is an invariant. However, in 1974 Perko discovered a counterexample called the [[Perko pair]], a pair of knots listed as distinct in tables for many years that are in fact the same.
* [[Hilbert's twenty-first problem]]. In 1908 [[Josip Plemelj|Plemelj]] claimed to have shown the existence of [[Fuchsian differential equation|Fuchsian]] [[differential equation]]s with any given [[monodromy]] group, but in 1989 [[Andrei Bolibrukh|Bolibruch]] discovered a counterexample.
* In 1925 [[Wilhelm Ackermann|Ackermann]] published a proof that a weak system can prove the consistency of a version of analysis, but [[John von Neumann|von Neumann]] found an explicit mistake in it a few years later. [[Gödel's incompleteness theorems]] showed that it is not possible to prove the consistency of analysis using weaker systems.
* Groups of order 64. In 1930 Miller published a paper claiming that there are 294 groups of order 64. [[Marshall Hall (mathematician)|Hall]] and Senior showed in 1964 that the correct number is 267.
* [[Kurt Gödel]] proved in 1933 that the truth of a certain class of sentences of [[first-order arithmetic]], known in the literature as <nowiki>[</nowiki>∃<sup>*</sup>∀<sup>2</sup>∃<sup>*</sup>,&nbsp;''all'',&nbsp;(0)<nowiki>]</nowiki>, was [[decidability (logic)|decidable]].  That is, there was a method for deciding correctly whether any statement of that form was true.  In the final sentence of that paper, he asserted that the same proof would work for the decidability of the larger class  <nowiki>[</nowiki>∃<sup>*</sup>∀<sup>2</sup>∃<sup>*</sup>,&nbsp;''all'',&nbsp;(0)<nowiki>]</nowiki><sub>=</sub>, which also includes formulas that contain an equality predicate.  However, in the mid-1960s, [[Stål Aanderaa]] showed that Gödel's proof would ''not'' go through for the larger class, and in 1982 [[Warren Goldfarb]] showed that validity of formulas from the larger class was in fact undecidable.<ref>{{cite book|title = The Classical Decision Problem | last1 = Boerger | first1 = Egon |last2=Grädel |first2= Erich |last3= Gurevich |first3=Yuri | page = 188 | publisher = Springer | year =  1997| isbn = 3-540-42324-9}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Feferman |editor-first=Solomon |editor-link=Solomon Feferman|title = Kurt Gödel: Collected Works | volume = 1 | last = Goldfarb | first = Warren | author-link = Warren Goldfarb | pages = 229–231 | publisher = Oxford University Press | year =  1986 | isbn = 0-19-503964-5 }}</ref>
* [[Grunwald–Wang theorem]]. [[Wilhelm Grunwald]] published an incorrect proof in 1933 of an incorrect theorem, and George Whaples later published another incorrect proof. [[Shianghao Wang]] found a counterexample in 1948 and published a corrected version of the theorem in 1950.
* In 1934 [[Francesco Severi|Severi]] claimed that the [[Chow group|space of rational equivalence classes of cycles]] on an [[algebraic surface]] is finite-dimensional, but {{harvtxt|Mumford|1968}} showed that this is false for surfaces of positive geometric genus.
* [[Jacobian conjecture]]. [[Ott-Heinrich Keller|Keller]] asked this as a question in 1939, and in the next few years there were several published incomplete proofs, including 3 by B. Segre, but [[Anatoli Georgievich Vitushkin|Vitushkin]] found gaps in many of them. More incomplete proofs were later announced. {{harvs|txt | last1=Bass | first1=Hyman | last2=Connell | first2=Edwin H. | last3=Wright | first3=David | year=1982 }} discuss the errors in some of these incomplete proofs. In 2026, [[Levent Alpöge]] found a counterexample for all n > 2.
* One of many examples from algebraic geometry in the first half of the 20th century: {{harvtxt|Severi|1946}} claimed that  a degree-''n'' surface in 3-dimensional projective space has at most ({{su|b=3|p=''n''+2}})−4 nodes, [[Beniamino Segre|B. Segre]] pointed out that this was wrong; for example, for degree 6 the maximum number of nodes is 65, achieved by the [[Barth sextic]], which is more than the maximum of 52 claimed by Severi.
* [[Rokhlin invariant]]. [[Vladimir Abramovich Rokhlin|Rokhlin]] incorrectly claimed in 1951 that the third stable stem of the [[homotopy groups of spheres]] is of order 12. In 1952 he discovered his error: it is in fact cyclic of order 24. The difference is crucial as it results in the existence of the Rokhlin invariant, a fundamental tool in the theory of 3- and 4-dimensional [[manifold]]s.
* In 1961, Jan-Erik Roos published an incorrect theorem about the vanishing of the first [[derived functor]] of the [[inverse limit]] [[functor]] under certain general conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal | last=Roos | first=Jan-Erik | author-link=Jan-Erik Roos | title=Sur les foncteurs dérivés de lim. Applications. | journal=C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris | mr=0132091 | year=1961 | volume=252 | pages=3702–3704}}</ref> However, in 2002, [[Amnon Neeman]] constructed a counterexample.<ref>{{Cite journal | last=Neeman | first=Amnon | title= A counterexample to a 1961 "theorem" in homological algebra| journal= Inventiones Mathematicae| mr=1906154 | year=2002 | volume=148 | pages=397–420 |issue=2 | doi=10.1007/s002220100197| bibcode=2002InMat.148..397N | s2cid=121186299 }}</ref> Roos  showed in 2006 that the theorem holds if one adds the assumption that the [[Category (mathematics)|category]] has a set of [[Generator (mathematics)|generators]].<ref>{{Citation | last=Roos | first=Jan-Erik | author-link=Jan-Erik Roos | title=Derived functors of inverse limits revisited | journal=[[London Mathematical Society|J. London Math. Soc.]] |series=Series 2 | mr=2197371  | year=2006 | volume=73 | issue=1 | pages=65–83 | doi=10.1112/S0024610705022416| s2cid=122666355 }}</ref>
* The [[Schur multiplier]] of the [[Mathieu group M22|Mathieu group M<sub>22</sub>]] is particularly notorious as it was miscalculated more than once: {{harvtxt|Burgoyne|Fong|1966}} first claimed it had order 3, then in a 1968 correction claimed it had order 6; its order is in fact (currently believed to be) 12. This caused an error in the title of [[Zvonimir Janko|Janko]]'s paper ''A new finite simple group of order 86,775,570,046,077,562,880 which possesses M<sub>24</sub> and the full covering group of M<sub>22</sub> as subgroup'' on [[Janko group J4|J4]]: it does not have the full covering group as a subgroup, as the full covering group is larger than was realized at the time.
* The original statement of the classification of [[N-groups]] by [[John G. Thompson|Thompson]] in 1968 accidentally omitted the [[Tits group]], though he soon fixed this.
* In 1975, Leitzel, Madan, and Queen incorrectly claimed that there are only 7 function fields over [[finite field]]s with genus >&thinsp;0 and class number 1, but in 2013 Stirpe found another; there are in fact exactly 8.
* [[Busemann–Petty problem]]. Zhang published two papers in the ''[[Annals of Mathematics]]'' in 1994 and 1999, in the first of which he proved that the Busemann–Petty problem in '''R'''<sup>4</sup> has a negative solution, and in the second of which he proved that it has a positive solution.
* [[Algebraic stack]]s. The book {{harvtxt|Laumon|Moret-Bailly|2000}} on algebraic stacks mistakenly claimed that [[morphism]]s of algebraic stacks induce morphisms of lisse-étale [[topos|topoi]]. The results depending on this were repaired by {{harvtxt|Olsson|2007}}.

==Theories proven inconsistent==
* [[Gottlob Frege|Frege]]'s [[foundations of mathematics]] in his 1879 book ''[[Begriffsschrift]]'' turned out to be inconsistent because of [[Russell's paradox]], found in 1901.
* [[Alonzo Church|Church]]'s original published attempt in 1932 to define a formal system was inconsistent, as was his correction in 1933. The consistent part of his system later became the [[lambda calculus]].
* [[Willard Van Orman Quine|Quine]] published his original description of the system [[New Foundations|Mathematical Logic]] in 1940, but in 1942 [[J. Barkley Rosser|Rosser]] showed it was inconsistent. [[Hao Wang (academic)|Wang]] found a correction in 1950; the consistency of this revised system is still unclear.
* In 1967 Reinhardt proposed [[Reinhardt cardinal]]s, which [[Kenneth Kunen|Kunen]] showed to be inconsistent with ZFC in 1971, though they are not known to be inconsistent with [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory|ZF]].
* [[Per Martin-Löf]]'s original version of [[intuitionistic type theory]] proposed in 1971 was shown to be inconsistent by [[Jean-Yves Girard]] in 1972, and was replaced by a corrected version.

==Status unclear==
* [[Uniform convergence]]. In his ''[[Cours d'Analyse]]'' of 1821, [[Augustin Cauchy|Cauchy]] "proved" that if a sum of [[continuous function]]s [[pointwise convergence|converges pointwise]], then its limit is also continuous.  However, [[Niels Henrik Abel|Abel]] observed in 1826 that this is not the case.  For the conclusion to hold, "pointwise convergence" must be replaced with "[[uniform convergence]]". It is not entirely clear that Cauchy's original result was wrong, because his definition of pointwise convergence was a little vague and may have been stronger than the one currently in use, and there are ways to interpret his result so that it is correct.<ref>{{cite book | title = The Cambridge History of Science | url = https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory07port | url-access = limited | last = Porter | first = Roy | page = [https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory07port/page/n504 476] | publisher = Cambridge University Press | year = 2003 | isbn = 0-521-57199-5|author-link=Roy Porter}}</ref>  There are many counterexamples using the standard definition of pointwise convergence.   For example, a [[Fourier series]] of [[sine]] and [[cosine]] functions, all continuous, may converge pointwise to a discontinuous function such as a [[step function]].
* [[Carmichael's totient function conjecture]] was stated as a theorem by [[Robert Daniel Carmichael]] in 1907, but in 1922 he pointed out that his proof was incomplete. As of 2016 the problem is still open.
* [[Italian school of algebraic geometry]]. Most gaps in proofs are caused either by a subtle technical oversight, or before the 20th century by a lack of precise definitions. A major exception to this is the Italian school of algebraic geometry in the first half of the 20th century, where lower standards of rigor gradually became acceptable. The result was that there are many papers in this area where the proofs are incomplete, or the theorems are not stated precisely. This list  contains a few representative examples, where the result was not just incompletely proved but also hopelessly wrong.
* In 1933 [[George David Birkhoff]] and Waldemar Joseph Trjitzinsky published a very general theorem<ref name=bitrj>{{cite journal|author=G. D. Birkhoff and W. J. Trjitzinsky|title=Analytic theory of singular difference equations|journal=Acta Math.|year=1933|volume=60|issue=1|pages=1–89|doi=10.1007/BF02398269|s2cid=121809579|doi-access=free}}</ref> on the asymptotics of sequences satisfying linear recurrences. The theorem was popularized by Jet Wimp and [[Doron Zeilberger]] in 1985.<ref name=wizeil>{{cite journal|author=J. Wimp and D. Zeilberger|title=Resurrecting the asymptotics of linear recurrences|journal=J. Math. Anal. Appl.|year=1985|volume=111|issue=1|pages=162–176|doi=10.1016/0022-247X(85)90209-4|doi-access=free}}</ref> However, while the result is probably true, as of now (2021) Birkhoff and Trjitzinsky's proof is not generally accepted by experts, and the theorem is (acceptedly) proved only in special cases.<ref name=flajsedg>{{cite book|author=P. Flajolet and R. Sedgewick|title=Analytic Combinatorics|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2009|url=http://algo.inria.fr/flajolet/Publications/AnaCombi/anacombi.html|pages=582/683|isbn=9780521898065}}</ref>
* A strengthening of [[Hilbert's sixteenth problem]] asking whether there exists a uniform finite upper bound for the number of limit cycles of planar polynomial vector fields of given degree ''n''. In the 1950s, [[Evgenii Landis]] and [[Ivan Petrovsky]] published a purported solution, but it was shown wrong in the early 1960s.<ref name=ilu/>
* In 1954  [[Kazimierz Zarankiewicz|Zarankiewicz]] claimed to have solved [[Turán's brick factory problem]] about the crossing number of [[complete bipartite graph]]s, but [[Paul Chester Kainen|Kainen]] and [[Gerhard Ringel|Ringel]] later noticed a gap in his proof.
* Complex structures on the 6-sphere. In 1969 Alfred Adler published a paper in the [[American Journal of Mathematics]] claiming that the 6-sphere has no complex structure. His argument was incomplete, and this is (as of 2016) still a major open problem.
* [[Closed geodesic]]s. In 1978 [[Wilhelm Klingenberg]] published a proof that smooth [[closed manifold|compact manifolds without boundary]] have infinitely many closed geodesics. His proof was controversial, and there is currently (as of 2016) no consensus on whether his proof is complete.
*In 1991, Kapranov and Voevodsky published a paper claiming to prove a version of the [[homotopy hypothesis]]. Later, Simpson showed the result of the paper is not true but conjectured that a variant of the result might be true, the variant now known as the [[Simpson conjecture]].
* [[Telescope conjecture]]. [[Douglas Ravenel|Ravenel]] announced a refutation of this in 1992, but later withdrew it, and the conjecture is still open.
* Matroid bundles. In 2003 [[Daniel Biss]] published a paper in the Annals of Mathematics claiming to show that matroid bundles are equivalent to real vector bundles, but in 2009 published a correction pointing out a serious gap in the proof.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://math.stackexchange.com/q/1955665 |title = Geometry - Has anyone ever actually seen this Daniel Biss paper?}}</ref> His correction was based on a 2007 paper by Mnëv.<ref>{{Cite arXiv |last=Mnev |first=N. |date=2007 |title=On D.K. Biss' papers 'The homotopy type of the matroid Grassmannian' and 'Oriented matroids, complex manifolds, and a combinatorial model for BU' |class=math.CO |eprint=0709.1291}}</ref>
* In 2012, the Japanese mathematician [[Shinichi Mochizuki]] released online a series of papers in which he claims to prove the [[abc conjecture]]. Despite the publication in a peer-reviewed journal later, his proof has not been accepted as correct in the mainstream mathematical community.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bordg |first=Anthony |date=December 2021 |title=A Replication Crisis in Mathematics? |journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer |language=en |volume=43 |issue=4 |pages=48–52 |doi=10.1007/s00283-020-10037-7 |issn=0343-6993 |pmc=8700325 |pmid=34966193}}</ref><ref>James Douglas Boyd, [https://www.sci-sci.org/_files/ugd/e7f2c3_babfab84a56e45fe9e78670028015817.pdf Inter-Universal Teichmüller Theory: Inside the Controversy]</ref>
